items.title: High gearing is risk, not failure
items.claim: A firm has long-term debt of £40 million and equity of £60 million. Its gearing ratio (debt / debt+equity) is 40%. Which statement is most accurate?

options.text: Gearing this high is always dangerous
Higher gearing magnifies returns to shareholders in good times and losses in bad — utilities routinely run 60%+ because cash flows are stable
Equity is always cheaper than debt

items.reveal:
UK water and electricity utilities (Severn Trent, National Grid) often carry gearing above 60% because regulated cash flows make debt servicing predictable. Tech firms (pre-2022) often had near-zero gearing because cash flows were volatile and equity was cheap.

Modigliani and Miller (1958) argued that, in perfect markets, capital structure is irrelevant. In real markets — with taxes, bankruptcy costs and asymmetric information — there is an optimal range. Lehman Brothers' gearing reached above 30:1 (debt:equity) before its 2008 collapse.
items.why: Whether high gearing is reckless depends on what cash flows look like. The number alone tells you little.

items.title: Break-even with multiple products needs a sales mix
items.claim: A bakery sells two products. Bread has £2 contribution per unit; cakes have £5. Fixed costs are £14,000. Without knowing the sales mix, what can you calculate?

options.text: You cannot calculate one break-even point — only break-even combinations or a break-even assuming a fixed sales mix ratio
Break-even is always the average contribution divided into fixed costs
You need the selling price as well

items.reveal:
If the bakery historically sells 3 loaves per cake, weighted contribution per 'bundle' = 3 x £2 + 1 x £5 = £11. Break-even = £14,000 / £11 = 1,273 bundles = 3,820 loaves + 1,273 cakes.

Change the mix and the break-even quantity changes. This is why textbook single-product break-even questions are misleading guides to multi-product reality. Real firms use 'weighted contribution' or 'break-even sales value' instead.
items.why: The simple Y = a + bX break-even chart assumes one product. Few real firms have only one product, which is why management accounting moves to contribution margin analysis.
